sentences.text: Austroraptor was a large, bipedal carnivore reaching lengths of 5 to 6 meters and weighing between 300 and 520 kilograms.
Its skull measured 80 centimeters in length, appearing low and elongated, which was significantly longer than those of other dromaeosaurids.
The animal possessed a long, low snout filled with numerous small, conical teeth that lacked serrations, a condition similar to that seen in spinosaurids.
A notable anatomical feature was its relatively short forearms when compared to most members of its group.
This dinosaur ranks among the largest known paravian dinosaurs and is the biggest dromaeosaurid discovered in the Southern Hemisphere.
Only Achillobator, Dakotaraptor, and Utahraptor are known to exceed its size.
The holotype specimen was collected in 2002 by Fernando Novas's team from the Museo Argentino de Ciencias Naturales in the Bajo de Santa Rosa locality.
Fernando Novas, Diego Pol, Juan Canale, Juan Porfiri, and Jorge Calvo formally named the genus and species A. cabazai in 2008.
Currently, there are two recorded fossil occurrences of this species.
Researchers suggest that unenlagiines like Austroraptor had superior running and pursuit predation capabilities compared to other dromaeosaurids.
In 2021, Brum and colleagues proposed that Austroraptor likely consumed fish as a significant or primary part of its diet.
The animal shared its paleoenvironment with early mammals, pterosaurs, and the titanosaurs Saltasaurus and Rocasaurus, which may have served as prey.
A 2012 comparison with a second sample revealed that the fourth toe was not especially wide and the supposed second phalanx was actually a first phalanx.
The discovery suggests that large coelurosaurs became common in the Late Cretaceous after the dominance of carcharodontosaurids declined.
Austroraptor is the youngest record of dromaeosaurids found in Gondwana and represents a previously unknown lineage of large predators in the late Cretaceous fauna.
Cladistic analysis places Austroraptor within the subfamily Unenlagiinae of the family Dromaeosauridae.
Austroraptor lived during the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous period in the Allen Formation of Argentina.
Thomas R. Holtz Jr. estimated that the animal lived between 78 and 66 million years ago.
The time range for Austroraptor is the Maastrichtian, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
Some researchers have hypothesized that the holotype specimen of Austroraptor might be a paleontological chimera, though this remains unproven.
